mainEntity.name: Are flexible dentures more comfortable than traditional dentures?

acceptedAnswer.text: Many patients find flexible dentures more comfortable than traditional rigid acrylic dentures, particularly because the soft, pliable material adapts to mouth movements and reduces pressure on the gums. However, comfort is subjective and depends on individual anatomy, the extent of tooth loss, and how well the denture has been fitted. Whether flexible dentures are the most suitable option for a particular patient is something that can only be determined through a clinical assessment by a qualified dental professional.

mainEntity.name: Can I sleep with my flexible dentures in?

acceptedAnswer.text: Most dental professionals advise removing dentures at night to allow the gum tissue to rest and recover from the pressure of wearing them during the day. This also reduces the risk of bacterial build-up and gum irritation. Your dentist will provide specific guidance based on your individual circumstances, as recommendations may vary depending on the type of denture and the health of your oral tissues. Always follow the advice of your dental team.

mainEntity.name: Will my flexible dentures need to be replaced over time?

acceptedAnswer.text: Flexible dentures are not designed to be a permanent solution and typically require replacement or relining over time. As the underlying gum tissue and bone change, the fit of the denture may alter. Most flexible dentures last between five and ten years with appropriate care, though this varies between individuals. Regular dental reviews help identify when adjustments or replacements may be appropriate. Your dentist can advise on the expected lifespan based on your specific denture and oral health status.

mainEntity.name: What should I do if my flexible denture breaks or becomes damaged?

acceptedAnswer.text: If your flexible denture cracks, fractures, or becomes visibly damaged, you should contact your dental practice as soon as possible. Do not attempt to repair the denture yourself using adhesives or DIY kits, as this can cause further damage or result in an ill-fitting appliance that may harm the gum tissue. Your dentist or dental technician will assess the damage and advise on repair or replacement options. A spare set of dentures may be worth discussing with your dental team if reliance on the appliance is a significant concern.

mainEntity.name: Is it normal to feel self-conscious about speaking with flexible dentures at first?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, this is a very common experience, particularly in the first two to three weeks. Changes in speech are a normal part of the adjustment period and occur because the tongue, lips, and cheeks are adapting to working around the new appliance. Practising reading aloud, speaking slowly and deliberately, and having supportive conversations with friends or family can help build confidence. For the vast majority of patients, speech returns to a natural pattern as the mouth adapts — this is a temporary phase rather than a lasting difficulty.

mainEntity.name: Can flexible dentures be relined if the fit changes?

acceptedAnswer.text: Whether a flexible denture can be relined depends on the specific material it is made from and the nature of the fit change. Some flexible denture materials are compatible with relining procedures, while others may require replacement if the fit has significantly altered. This is something that requires professional assessment — your dentist will be able to advise on the most appropriate course of action based on the condition of your denture and the changes to your gum tissue or bone.
